title: Sell Mineral Rights in Baker, MT
metaTitle: Sell Mineral Rights in Baker, MT
metaDescription: Baker, MT is the site of one of Montana's first oil discoveries and the Fallon County seat. A retired engineer explains what that century-old history means for your minerals.
heroLead: Baker had a producing oil well before most of the Bakken counties existed as an idea, and that 1919 discovery is still the reference point for anything I evaluate here.
intro: As the Fallon County seat, Baker is where the courthouse records for the surrounding Cedar Creek Anticline sit, and that anticline is genuinely historic ground. The discovery well drilled near town in 1919 was one of Montana's first commercial oil strikes, targeting shallower conventional zones rather than the shale that made headlines eighty years later. A lot of mineral title in and around Baker has been through multiple rounds of leasing since then, which makes the paper trail worth real attention.

sections.heading: A Century of Layered Leasing
paragraphs: When a field has been producing since 1919, chances are your family's interest has been leased, released, and re-leased more than once, sometimes to different operators targeting different zones at different times. I've pulled Fallon County title files that show three or four distinct leasing episodes across a single tract. Sorting out which lease is currently active and what your net revenue interest actually is under that lease takes real courthouse work, not a guess based on an old document in a family file.

sections.heading: Cedar Creek Anticline Versus the Newer Bakken Edge
paragraphs: Baker-area production has historically come from the Red River and Charles formations along the anticline, conventional targets that decline slowly and predictably compared to a shale well. Newer Bakken and Three Forks interest does extend toward this part of Fallon County from the more active core farther north, but it's thinner here, and I check current permitting specifically before assuming your tract has both kinds of potential.

sections.heading: What I'd Look At for a Baker-Area Tract
paragraphs: I start with your current division order if you're already receiving royalty, compare it against the recorded chain of title, and check the well's production decline over the last few years. For undeveloped acreage nearby, I look at whether it's closer to the older Cedar Creek trend or the newer Bakken-edge activity, since that shapes which buyers are actually interested and at what range.

faqs.question: Why is Baker, MT significant to Montana's oil history?
faqs.answer: The Cedar Creek Anticline discovery well near Baker in 1919 was one of the first commercial oil strikes in the state, decades before the Bakken shale play developed. Production along this trend has continued, in slow decline, for over a century.

faqs.question: Is my Baker-area mineral interest Cedar Creek Anticline or Bakken?
faqs.answer: It could be either, or both. Pull your lease and division order history at the Fallon County Clerk and Recorder in Baker to see which formation your current production, if any, comes from.

faqs.question: Why does an old well from decades ago still pay royalties?
faqs.answer: Conventional fields like those along the Cedar Creek Anticline decline slowly and can produce economically for many decades. A modest, steady royalty check from an old well is a real, valuable asset even without new drilling.
